summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity. Its national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. El Callao stands under that national framework: no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding appears in the sources, so what a trans visitor faces in this department is what the national rules deliver.

The governing instrument is the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Its Article 5.1 prohibits any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities. The plenary of Congress approved the text and waived a second vote on 2 April 2025. The same package obliges venues not to post ambiguous or inclusive restroom signage. The bills were merged and approved by unanimity in the Comision de Mujer y Familia on 20 February 2025, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante of Honor y Democracia; the stated trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

Enforcement rests on individuals judging appearance and documents. Activist Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, states that security staff would have to check the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. The restriction already reaches private premises: the consumer-protection body INDECOPI, in SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which had grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases across 2020-2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. A 2024 report co-authored by Gianna Camacho found hate crimes rising with trans women most affected and stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

One case illustrates the pattern of targeted killing: in February 2023 the 31-year-old trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot. Two killers were arrested in March 2023.

Peru's crime-registration systems do not incorporate sexual orientation or gender identity, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 of the April 2025 law as a direct breach of Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Restriction of speech and association runs alongside the facilities ban. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Two protective developments are on record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack; it was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains a long, costly and invasive process, which shapes how residents obtain documents matching their identity and how readily they can invoke them against restroom enforcement.

In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings.

Residents live without hate-crime coverage: the 2017 repeal carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote, and amid a petition claiming one million signatures, removed LGBT protections from the Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, and no later restoration appears in the sources.

The censorship provisions of the April 2025 law bind residents' media, advertising, artistic and educational output, and the obscenity minimum sentence now stands at four years.
outOfScopeNotes:
No El Callao-specific source content was located: the three sources cited for this department contain no reference to El Callao, so the local picture is unresolved rather than confirmed as matching or diverging from the national pattern.

The violence figures are national aggregates with no department-level breakdown, so the distribution of the 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases across El Callao is not sourced.

Whether the April 2025 restroom provision has produced documented enforcement actions, complaints or refusals inside El Callao is not sourced; the only enforcement example on record, the SmartFit dismissal, is a Lima-area case.

The claim that recorded hate-crime figures are a sub-registry rests on Gianna Camacho's assessment and cannot be quantified from the inventory.
